nameStory: The Hooded Tube Lichen gets its name from the distinctive way its leaf-like lobes curl upward at the edges, creating little hoods or cups. This gives it a monk's cowl appearance, which is why it's also called monk's-hood lichen. The "tube" part refers to the hollow structure of each lobe - they're not solid but form tiny tubes when you look at them from the side.
description: Hooded Tube Lichen is a leafy, grey-green lichen that forms large, irregular patches on tree bark and rocks. It's loosely attached to its surface, almost like it's draped over its host rather than glued down tight. The individual lobes are hollow tubes about 2-3mm wide that often curl upward at their edges, giving the whole patch a ruffled appearance. This is one of New England's most common lichens, often covering substantial areas of bark.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Leafy lobes that are hollow like tiny tubes, loosely attached and often curling upward at the edges like little hoods

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grey to yellowish-green on top when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; black and wrinkled underneath with brown edges

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface often dotted with tiny black specks like pepper flakes, giving it a speckled appearance

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: White powdery soredia frequently visible on the undersides of upturned lobe edges, like flour dusting

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are 2-3mm wide but patches can spread to cover large areas of bark, sometimes hand-sized or bigger

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Most commonly found on tree bark, especially conifers, but also grows on rocks and old wood

habitat: You'll find Hooded Tube Lichen throughout New England's forests, from sea level to mountain elevations. It's especially common on the bark of conifers like spruce, fir, and pine, but also grows on hardwoods, rocks, and old wooden structures. Look for it in both mature forests and younger woodlands - it's quite adaptable to different forest conditions.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as spring moisture returns. The contrast between the green upper surface and black undersides is particularly striking when wet from spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Often appears more greyish during dry spells, but maintains its distinctive hooded shape. Summer humidity can bring out the green coloration on foggy mornings.
seasonality.fall: Color may shift more toward yellowish-green. Fall rains revive the bright green appearance and make the white soredia more visible on lobe edges.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible and identifiable even under light snow. The grey winter coloration makes the black pepper-spot markings more obvious against the pale background.

funFact: This lichen is like a natural air quality monitor - scientists use it to detect air pollution because it's moderately sensitive to sulfur dioxide and heavy metals, so healthy populations indicate cleaner air in your area.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other grey-green leafy lichens, but the hollow, tube-like lobes that curl upward are unique. Remember: if the edges hood up like tiny monks' cowls and the lobes feel hollow when gently squeezed, you've found your Hooded Tube Lichen.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "monk's-hood lichen," this has no relation to the poisonous monkshood plant. The name simply refers to the hood-like shape of the curled lobe edges that resemble a monk's cowl or hood.
compareHints: Unlike its tube lichen relatives, Hooded Tube Lichen has those distinctive pepper-like black dots scattered across its surface and more pronounced upward-curling edges. Freckled Tube Lichen lacks the abundant black specks, while Powder-headed Tube Lichen has more soredia concentrated at the lobe tips rather than along the edges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Freckled Tube Lichen differs from Hooded Tube Lichen by having scattered dark spots rather than smooth surfaces, and from Powder-headed Tube Lichen by lacking the powdery white soredia (reproductive dust) at the lobe tips.
Among the tube lichens in New England, Powder-headed Tube Lichen has the most inflated, balloon-like lobes compared to its relatives.
Unlike its relative the Hooded Tube Lichen which has more inflated, hood-like lobes, Lattice Tube Lichen has distinctly hollow, narrower tubes.
